detail.abstract: Option portfolios are exposed to the joint tail of the underlying index and its implied volatility, and the shape of that joint tail plausibly changes with market conditions. This study examines whether conditioning extreme value marginals and copula dependence on a latent market regime improves one-and two-session forecasts of Value-at-Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES) for option books driven by the S&P 500 index (SPX) and the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX). The proposed regime-dependent EVT-copula model combines a three-state Gaussian hidden Markov model fitted to returns and realized volatility, AR(1)-GJR-GARCH(1,1) filters with Student-t innovations, generalized Pareto tails spliced to weighted empirical centres, and a profile-likelihood Student-t copula estimated separately in each state. It is compared with historical simulation, GARCH filtered historical simulation, a static EVT-copula and regimeweighted historical simulation on four hypothetical, model-priced 30-day European books: a long straddle, a short strangle, a protective put and a bear put spread. Forecasts are generated in a strict expanding-window walk-forward design with monthly refits, filtered (never smoothed) out-of-sample state probabilities and explicit, reported scenario-support bounds, and are evaluated with coverage tests, a HAC joint VaR-ES calibration test and the strictly consistent Fissler-Ziegel score with Holm-adjusted Diebold-Mariano comparisons. A controlled simulation with known regimes validates the pipeline over 504 out-of-sample sessions. The filtered state model separates simulated stress days with an area under the ROC curve of 0.94, and the regime-dependent EVT-copula records no Kupiec rejection across 24 portfolio, horizon and confidence cells, attains the lowest average joint VaR-ES score, and is never significantly worse than any competitor. All 17 Holm-significant score differences favour it, concentrated in the short-gamma strangle and the protective put at the 99% level; no advantage appears for the long straddle. On 1,673 out-of-sample SPX/VIX sessions from January 2020 to August 2026 the proposed model is well calibrated, with no Kupiec or conditional-coverage rejection in any cell, and significantly outperforms historical simulation and regime-weighted historical simulation. Under the Fissler-Ziegel score it does not beat the static EVT-copula or GARCH filtered historical simulation, which rank first and second, and it is significantly worse than both for the short strangle, because its stress-state Expected Shortfall is conservative. The static EVT-copula ranks first in all ten fully executed, pre-declared robustness variants, including a rerun with wider scenario supports, and the regime model comes closest with two states; a joint block bootstrap shows that state-specific tail differences are imprecisely estimated. The regime signal itself is informative: days it flags in advance (31% of the sample) contain 71% to 94% of the worst 1% of losses, and on those days the proposed model has the breach rate closest to nominal. The evidence positions regime conditioning as a real-time stress-detection and capital-prudence overlay on a filtered EVT-copula engine, trading false alarms for stress-day coverage, rather than as a universal improvement in average scoring-rule accuracy. All option marks come from Black-Scholes at a flat volatility equal to VIX/100, which ignores the volatility smile, skew and term structure; the study is a reproducible model-marking laboratory, not a historical optionmarket backtest, and validation on observed implied-volatility surfaces is the essential next step.

detail.abstract: The term price stability commonly refers to efforts by the Federal Reserve to "target" a rate of price inflation that promotes real economic growth and maximum employment. Price stability in the classic sense, however, describes the inherent tendency of a market to reestablished price equilibrium following a demand-side or supply-side shock. This paper investigates the inflationary dynamics of four Federal Reserve chairs. The analysis confirms that price stability in the classic sense was not a goal of monetary policy. Instead, monetary policy was one of several sources of money market shocks and that price stability in the classic sense provided the economy with a measure of protection that has limited the harmful effects of faulty Fed policies from spiraling out of control.

detail.abstract: Many of my basketball research ideas failed to produce the findings I expected, and I kept the records. This paper tests whether an AI agent can use those records to decide whether a new research idea is worth pursuing. Five language models evaluated ten historical research proposals using only information available when each was originally proposed. The experiments compared decisions made without an archive, with keyword-based document and graph search over taskspecific snapshots of a 319-family research archive, and with embedding-based retrieval. A separate experiment supplied relevant earlier studies directly, with and without notes explaining when their lessons applied. The evaluation used a fixed answer key based on the archive's recorded outcome classifications: proposals associated with untestable or artifact findings were classified as stop decisions; other outcomes were classified as go decisions. Thus, the experiment tests prediction of researchdesign failure under this archive's classification rules, not general research judgment. Access to the archive did not reliably improve decisions. Across 300 paired comparisons, memory corrected 47 wrong decisions but also introduced 46 errors. Models generally reproduced the recorded outcome statuses of studies they cited, but did not reliably determine when those studies applied to a new proposal. The same data-quality record could support opposite decisions for two proposals, illustrating the difficulty of transferring lessons across research contexts. Embedding retrieval found relevant earlier studies substantially more often than keyword search, but did not improve decision accuracy. Directly supplying relevant studies produced higher accuracy for four of the five models, although ten proposals are insufficient to establish whether this difference is reliable. The findings suggest that retrieving organizational research history is not enough: AI agents must also determine when prior findings and limitations apply to new decisions. This distinction matters as organizations develop systems intended to preserve and reuse institutional knowledge. A larger evaluation involving 60 to 100 proposals is a necessary next step.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates gender gaps in early-career outcomes, namely stabilization into or exit from academia, and relates them to measures of female representation in the working environment. To this end, survival analysis is applied to administrative data covering the universe of entry-position researchers employed under fixed-term contracts at Italian universities between 2011 and 2026. We find that female scholars have a systematically lower probability of stabilizing with a tenured position compared to male scholars, while no gender gap is found in the likelihood of leaving academia before stabilization. We also find that greater female presence and a less pronounced glass ceiling are associated with higher probability of stabilization, especially for women, and with lower probability of exit, whereby in this case no significant difference is observed across genders. These findings suggest that gender inequalities in early academic careers are reflected more clearly in access to stable employment than in differential probabilities of leaving academia, and that more gender-balanced academic environments may lead to more equitable and inclusive career trajectories.

detail.abstract: We study Cournot competition on a transmission-constrained network between a profitmaximizing private generator and a less efficient public generator whose objective is a weighted average of consumers' surplus and own profit. This weight-a regulatory mandate and, equivalently, a measure of public ownership-constitutes the policy instrument; we derive its welfare-maximizing value as a function of relative efficiency and transmission capacity. When the network is uncongested, the mixed-oligopoly tradeoff applies: a positive weight on consumers' surplus is optimal only if the efficiency deficit is small; otherwise profit maximization is optimal. Under congestion, a more consumeroriented public firm reduces the output imbalance between generators, relieving the transmission constraint and allowing the more efficient private generator to expand. This congestion-relief effect can make a positive weight optimal even when this deficit would otherwise call for profit maximization. The optimal mandate and ownership structure thus depend on network capacity and relative production costs.

detail.abstract: I show that higher interest rates can increase bank leverage through loan losses. Before the Global Financial Crisis, contractionary monetary policy raises leverage by 5-10 percent and increases bank failures, even as lending contracts. I propose and validate the loan-loss channel of monetary policy, which explains the increase in leverage: contractionary shocks increase loan losses, reduce profits and equity, thus raising leverage. Microdata evidence supports the mechanism as banks with greater repricing exposure experience stronger pass-through to loan rates and subsequently larger loan losses, weaker profits, and higher leverage. These results reveal risk transformation: loan repricing shifts interest-rate risk from banks to borrowers but ultimately back to banks as credit risk. Post-crisis, loan losses still rise, but stronger net interest income offsets them, so leverage falls. My findings provide a direct link between monetary policy and financial stability: loan-rate pass-through affects borrower performance, shaping bank leverage and failure risk.

detail.abstract: Firms that build artificial intelligence into their products and decisions ask investors to value capabilities that outsiders cannot inspect. This paper theorizes why that opacity makes media sentiment a pivotal signal at the initial public offering, and why the signal works differently in China's capital market. Integrating the view of artificial intelligence as an entrepreneurial actor with dual processing, celebrity, and attribution theories, we propose that AI development raises positive media sentiment at a decreasing rate, that narrative and substance diverge as Knightian uncertainty grows, and that sentiment relates to post-listing performance in an inverted U whose turning point depends on the verifiability of AI claims. We further propose that registrationbased pricing, retail participation, official media endorsement, state ownership, and the attributional content of coverage condition these links. The framework recasts media sentiment as an interpretive bridge between technological opacity and investor valuation.

detail.abstract: Inflation is defined as a consistent rise in the overall cost of goods and services, leading to an overall decrease in purchasing power with each dollar leading to higher living costs for households. Using monthly and annual data derived from the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) collected by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) and Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) for the years 2020 through 2025, this paper will analyze overall inflation and the impact of three major necessities: food, housing (or shelter), and energy. Overall 12-month inflation peaked at 7.0% in December 2021 and 6.5% in December 2022 before dropping to 2.7% in December 2025. However, even despite this decrease, individuals are still seeing significant increases in the cost of housing (6.2% in 2023, 4.6% in 2024, and 3.2% in 2025) compared to pre-pandemic costs. Based on analyzing these data using microeconomic principles related to the consumer budget constraint, price elasticity of demand, and real purchasing power, individuals can determine how price shocks based on inelastic necessities lead to people (especially those with lower incomes) having to shift their budget away from nonessential purchases and saving.

detail.abstract: Privatization neutrality in mixed oligopoly fails under strict budget balance when the regulator can use only per-unit taxes and subsidies. We show that a revenue contest restores neutrality without relaxing budget balance. Each firm receives a fixed share of the excess of its revenue over its rivals' average and pays the same share of any shortfall. In the standard identical-cost setting and under suitable demand conditions, a single contest parameter uniquely implements the first best for every degree of privatization under simultaneous moves. Transfers always sum to zero and are individually zero at the first best. When demand is uncertain and the first-best demand elasticity is state-independent, as in the linear-quadratic and constant-elasticity cases, one contest implements the first best with a balanced budget in every state, whereas fixed per-unit, ad valorem and lump-sum transfers fail as soon as the public firm is even partially privatized.

detail.abstract: Rapid urbanization can cause a disconnect from nature, which affects ecological resilience and human wellbeing. Urban biophilia provides a technique to bring nature back into cities. With the use of social perception analysis, spatial mapping, and field surveys, this study evaluates Pokhara City, Nepal's current biophilic level. The study assessed existing biophilic infrastructure, institutional engagement, and public awareness using GPS (Global Positioning System) mapping, nursery observations (n = 12), household questionnaires (n = 60), and GIS (Geographic Information System) based analysis of green spaces. The findings show that while 87 percent of households have access to green space of some form, only 55 percent live close to parks that are accessible by walking within ten minutes. The level of biophilia remains low overall, with minimal green infrastructure, no cutting-edge greening technologies, and limited public involvement. Religious sites and cultural activities operate as informal biophilic areas, helping to make up for this gap. Despite their inadequate willingness to actively encourage greening, residents have concerns about urban greenery. The expansion of parks, the promotion of rooftop and vertical gardens, stricter enforcement of urban greening regulations, and increased public awareness are some of the policy recommendations. Sustainable urban development in Pokhara and other mid-sized cities is informed by the findings, which also add to the discourse on biophilic cities in South Asia.

detail.abstract: Embedded topic models integrate word embeddings into the topic generation process, producing coherent topics and robust performance on large vocabularies. However, each document is represented by a single topic distribution, ignoring its internal structure.  Many real world collections, including legal documents, company and government reports, and online discussion forums, exhibit hierarchical organization in which documents consist of multiple sections that often address distinct subtopics. We introduce the Hierarchical Embedded Topic Model (hETM), a structured topic model that couples the topic distribution of a document and those of its sections through a hierarchical prior in the embedding space. We derive an amortized variational inference procedure for hETM and evaluate it on structured collections from each of these domains. Experimental results show that hETM achieves the lowest or near-lowest held-out perplexity among flat and hierarchical topic model baselines, along with comparable or higher topic quality. It also performs strongly on a downstream clustering task, achieving the best clustering performance on most of the collections.

detail.abstract: Between 2004 and 2025 the private share of enrolment in Brazil’s compulsory fundamental cycle rose from 12.8 to 19.2 percent. It grew fastest, in proportional terms, among households of modest means, over a period in which public school quality improved in every state. This paper documents that migration with the annual PNAD (2004–2015) and the education module of the PNADc (2016–2025), and describes its correlates among 666,881 children aged 7 to 13, each matched to the lagged, stagespecific public IDEB score of their state. The two surveys are estimated separately, with state and year fixed effects. Household income is the strongest correlate: a 10 percent difference in income per capita accompanies a difference of about 1.5 percentage points in the probability of private attendance, against a mean of 15 percent. The mother’s completion of secondary school is the next strongest. A higher public IDEB, relative to the national change for the same stage, is associated with lower private attendance, clearly in the PNADc and more weakly in the PNAD. This association varies with income in an inverted U: estimated separately by income decile, it is weakest among the poorest children, strongest in the seventh to ninth deciles, and weaker again in the top decile, where two children in three attend private schools. The estimates are associations; they are effects only under assumptions the paper states and leaves to the reader to judge, and the projections that follow are credible only to a reader who accepts them. Projected to 2035 under constant private fees, the private share at these ages, 20 percent in 2025, would reach 22 to 25 percent if public quality stopped improving and 19 to 22 percent if it kept improving at its past rate, for income growth of 1 to 3 percent a year; combined with falling births, every scenario implies a fall in public enrolment of 12 to 20 percent while the constitutional earmark keeps public education spending tied to revenue, which motivates a means-tested, piloted voucher priced at the marginal cost of a public place.

detail.abstract: An article written by Felix Mormann in the Boston College Law Review argued for a normative theory in favor of automated regulation. This paper aims to redress his misunderstanding by examining the extensive literature on automated regulation in the public utility field as well as the significant history of experimentation with automated mechanisms. In responding to Mormann, this paper addresses a major area of interest over the past several decades for public utility commissioners in the U.S. and other countries. Public utility commissions over their history have deployed both formulaic and discretionary approaches, often grappling with what approach would better achieve just and reasonable rates. Legal statutes and court interpretations allow commissions much leeway in choosing one approach, depending on the economic, political and technological conditions that a utility faces. As this paper illustrates, one approach may be preferable under certain situations but not in others. Commissions frequently apply in their ratemaking function, and rightly so, a hybrid approach that incorporates both formulas and regulatory discretion to best achieve just and reasonable rates. Examples includes price caps and other multi-year rate plans, formula rates, and fuel adjustment clauses. Overall, this paper shows Mormann's argument that more automation in utility ratemaking would advance the public interest is presumptuous and dependent on the environment within which utilities operate.

detail.abstract: Armed groups in the Sahel increasingly fight by cutting supply lines. In September 2025, the jihadist group JNIM declared a blockade of fuel imports into Mali and destroyed tanker convoys on the main corridors. This paper measures what the blockade did to cereal markets, using recorded monthly prices from 133 markets (2015-2026), geocoded conflict events and 3,178 market pairs. The blockade did not raise average prices near the attacks. It raised the cost of distance: within the same market pair and month, price gaps for maize and rice, the cereals traded over long distances, rose with distance by 0.029 per log point more than gaps for millet and sorghum. None of 105 placebo start dates reproduces this effect (permutation p = 0.009). The paper contributes the first measure of the market effects of a blockade by a non-state armed group in Africa, and shows that machine-learning imputations of missing prices hide them. Early-warning systems that track average prices in reference markets miss this burden, which falls on households that depend on long-haul trade.

detail.abstract: Thailand's coastal regions are dealing with serious problems like flooding and sea level rise due to the effects of climate change. This study investigates the different adaptation measures for sea-level rise and flooding adaptation measures in Thailand. The paper starts with an introduction that outlines the topic's background and context, specifies the research question, and describes the study area of Thailand. The methodologies employed for the literature search are also presented. It then examines factors, such as physical, socioeconomic, governance, environmental, and technical aspects, that affect coastal vulnerability by drawing on a literature search of relevant papers. It also discusses different adaptation strategies for flooding and sea level rise, including natural ones like mangrove forests, coral reefs, and seagrass beds. It also discusses structural solutions like flood walls, water gates, and retention ponds, as well as nonstructural ones like early warning systems, evacuation plans, and emergency response teams. This paper emphasizes the significance of local and indigenous knowledge, community-based adaptation methods, and enhancing community resilience in coastal communities. Additionally, case studies of effective Thai adaptation strategies to climate change are presented. These investigations shed light on the difficulties, opportunities, and lessons uncovered from real-world coastal adaptation experiences in Thailand. detail.abstract: Measuring analyst bias as the gap between the consensus and a machine-learning forecast, I show that analysts and price correct that bias on different schedules. Analysts revise their forecasts mainly in the early post-announcement period, whereas prices respond to the bias primarily in the later period. A model in which investors place weight on analyst forecasts explains why belief correction can precede price correction. Consistent with this mechanism, greater analyst responsiveness to earnings news is associated with less subsequent pricing of bias. These findings show that price correction to bias depends not only on how analysts revise their forecasts, but also on how investors incorporate those forecasts into prices.

detail.abstract: Under CECL a lender may estimate its allowance for credit losses with any reasonable method, and the SEC expects it to document an identified range of expected losses. This paper measures how much of that range comes from the choice among equally accurate default models. On 49,406,273 Freddie Mac mortgages, at each of 21 year-ends from 2005 to 2025, I train 65 models on what a lender knew at the time, keep those within one bootstrap standard error of the best held-out log loss, and compute the lifetime allowance of the same portfolio under each, with the prepayment model, the economic forecast, the reversion policy and loss severity held fixed. The design and six predictions were recorded before the data were opened. Across these models the allowance ranges over a median of 55% of the most accurate model's (17% and 6% among the few models that a paired test at two or one standard errors cannot separate from the best), up to 18.0 billion dollars on Freddie Mac's active book, and more than the gap between one-and three-year reversion at every date. Realized losses fall inside the range at one of 13 dates: model uncertainty is not forecast uncertainty. The spread was not unusually large in relative terms before the crisis, and monotone constraints barely narrow it. Code and every aggregate result are released.

detail.abstract: In much of sub-Saharan Africa HIV is seen as the result of disapproved sexual behaviour, and the shame that follows is thought to keep people from testing. Between 2015 and 2021 the Demographic and Health Surveys asked about family shame and community stigma. This paper uses those questions to ask whether shame is associated with lower HIV testing, and how much of the gap in testing between rich and poor it accounts for. The sample is 300,979 women and men aged 15 to 49 in 16 countries. People who would be ashamed if a family member had HIV were about 5 percentage points less likely to have ever tested. The association was negative for both women and men in all 16 countries (32 separate estimates), significant in 25 of them, and stable across checks. Women tested less where shame was common in their community; for men this association was weak. Shame was more common among the poor in every country, but the gap in testing between ashamed and other respondents did not differ by wealth. Shame accounted for about 7% of wealth-related inequality in testing among men and 15% among women, against more than half for education. Antenatal testing hid much of the inequality among women: those without a recent birth resembled men. Respondents who knew that HIV is not spread by sharing food or by mosquitoes were 4 to 8 percentage points less likely to be ashamed. Shame is a consistent but moderate barrier to testing, and a small part of why the poor test less.

detail.abstract: Revenue mobilisation is essential to the capacity of government to finance public services, provide infrastructure, maintain economic stability, and support national development. In Nigeria, persistent challenges involving tax evasion, revenue leakages, administrative inefficiency, fragmented tax structures, inadequate taxpayer records, and weak institutional accountability have limited the effectiveness of public revenue administration. The growing use of digital technology offers opportunities to address these challenges through electronic tax filing, online payment platforms, automated assessment, taxpayer identification systems, electronic receipts, and datadriven compliance monitoring. However, digital transformation requires more than the introduction of technological platforms. It depends on institutional capacity, appropriate legislation, reliable infrastructure, data protection, transparency, and public confidence. This paper examines revenue authority reforms and digital tax collection in Nigeria, with particular attention to their implications for public sector accountability. It adopts a qualitative doctrinal and documentary research methodology, drawing on academic literature, legislation, institutional publications, and policy materials. The study examines the experiences of the former Federal Inland Revenue Service, the Lagos State Internal Revenue Service, and the Kwara State Internal Revenue Service, while considering the institutional changes introduced through Nigeria's 2025 tax reform legislation and the commencement of major tax laws in 2026. Institutional Theory and the Technology Acceptance Model provide the theoretical foundation. The paper finds that digital tax administration can improve revenue traceability, reduce manual interference, strengthen taxpayer records, and support more effective financial oversight. Nevertheless, inadequate infrastructure, limited digital literacy, institutional resistance, weak data management, cybersecurity risks, and insufficient public engagement continue to affect implementation. The paper recommends stronger institutional controls, integrated digital platforms, improved taxpayer education, transparent revenue reporting, effective regulatory coordination, and independent oversight. It concludes that digital tax collection can strengthen public sector accountability only when technological reforms are supported by responsible institutions, fair tax administration, and enforceable governance standards.

detail.abstract: Innovation adoption in project-based industries is shaped by fragmented delivery structures, distributed decision authority, professional liability, and limited opportunities for experimentation. Existing approaches provide valuable but partial insights: innovation adoption and project decision models explain staged progression, while innovation system frameworks explain the broader conditions supporting technological development and diffusion. This paper develops a phase-dependent framework for analysing innovation adoption in high-consequence project-based contexts by extending the Technological Innovation System (TIS) perspective to connect system-level conditions with adoption progression. The framework consolidates the seven classical TIS functions into four adapted functions: Knowledge Validation, Institutional Legitimacy, Demand Formation, and Implementation Capacity, capturing how system functions shape adoption within project evaluation, approval, and delivery. These functions are linked to a five-phase adoption process consisting of awareness, consideration, evaluation, decision, and implementation through diagnostic questions identifying inducement and blocking mechanisms across phases. The framework conceptualizes diffusion not as the outcome of uniformly strong system dynamics but as an emergent effect of repeated project-level progression. Under this view, functional fulfilment becomes phase dependent: support for innovation adoption may remain strong during some phases while weakening during others. Adoption failure is therefore interpreted not as general system weakness but as localized breakdowns in progression occurring at specific adoption stages. The framework provides a basis for analysing where adoption becomes constrained, which functions weaken across phases, and which mechanisms shape the diffusion of focal innovations within project-based innovation systems. In doing so, it helps identify intervention points to support innovation adoption and diffusion in high-consequence project-based environments.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a testable market microstructure framework for investigating whether historical volume concentration modifies the predictive information contained in deviations between realized price movements and order-flow-implied price impact. Existing research documents substantial relationships between order flow imbalance, market depth, and short-horizon price changes; the predictive importance of unexpected price responses, however, may depend on the historical distribution of executed volume across prices. In that proxy specification the interaction term provides no detectable incremental out-of-sample information and does not outperform placebo volume-location weights. Because the proxy cannot reproduce the order-flow specification, the pilot does not test the central hypothesis, which remains to be evaluated with order-book data.

detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of Nigeria’s intra-African trade flows disaggregated into exports and imports on economic growth within the framework of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). The motivation stems from the persistent disconnect between Nigeria’s expanding regional trade engagements and its modest growth outcomes. Using annual time-series data from 1983 to 2024, the study employs the Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) model to explore the short- and long-run dynamics between Nigeria’s intra-African exports, imports, and economic growth. The findings reveal that while both exports and imports exert a significant positive impact on economic growth in the long run, their short-run effects are limited by exchange rate volatility and a 40% speed of adjustment toward equilibrium. Notably, gross capital formation exerts a negative and persistent influence, highlighting structural bottlenecks in domestic investment. These results imply that while regional trade holds long-term promise, Nigeria’s current growth is hindered by high production costs and currency shocks. The study concludes that to fully benefit from AfCFTA, Nigeria must adopt the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) to mitigate exchange rate risks, reorient import composition toward productive intermediate inputs, and improve investment efficiency through trade-enabling infrastructure.

detail.abstract: AI agents increasingly act for people through chains of sub-agents, tools and adapters. Identity tells a relying party who acted, and authorization tells it what a token allowed, but neither shows whether what was actually executed stayed within what a person authorized. We present the Agentic Mandate Evidence Protocol (AMEP), an open specification for portable, signed evidence of each link in that chain (mandate, delegation, intent, interpretation, invocation, approval and an independently observed executed effect) and a deterministic, three-valued evaluation over it. The evaluation returns preserved, violated or unresolved, and every non-preserved result names one of eleven invariants. Missing or unverifiable evidence yields unresolved, never permission. Authority is modelled as claim sets with a decidable order and meet, so attenuation across delegation hops can be checked offline by any third party with public keys alone. We describe the design, the claim algebra and invariants, and a conformance suite of 95 vectors on which two independently written verifiers agree. We also report two integrations: an MCP extension prototype in which tool servers return signed receipts of the effects they actually executed, and a 20vector delegation suite mapped to an agent-identity registry protocol under discussion in a W3C Community Group. AMEP is published as an IETF Internet-Draft with open-source reference implementations.

detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence allows people to produce work that signals a level of expertise they cannot demonstrate on their own. This conceptual article calls the resulting condition expertise larping: performing expertise one does not possess while sincerely believing one possesses it. Drawing on research on metacognitive calibration, cognitive offloading, automation and skill decay, self-efficacy, and the emerging evidence on generative AI in learning and work, the article develops the Simulated Expertise Framework. Its seven constructs distinguish assisted performance from independent capability, define the simulation margin between them, and trace how source misattribution, inflated expertise self-perception, practice displacement, and capability drift connect. A proposed five-link mechanism, the simulation spiral, describes how a misattributed margin may lower the felt need for skill-building practice, how the AI absorbs that practice, and how independent capability may then stall or decay, widening the margin and weakening the capacity to verify AI output exactly where verification matters most. A typology separates four expertise states, distinguishing hazardous larping from legitimate, deliberate delegation. Seven propositions are stated with their evidence status and falsifying observations. The article then defines healthy use, termed capability augmentation, by two conditions rather than by the amount of AI use: self-perception remains calibrated to independent capability, and independent capability is maintained or grows. Five practices that operationalize these conditions are specified for individuals, educators, and organizations, together with a research agenda built on paired assisted and unassisted assessment.

detail.abstract: Aggregate credit growth does not by itself determine the direction of consumer prices: under the same aggregate expansion, consumer prices may strengthen or weaken according to the allocation of financing, income reflux, and supply response. This paper asks under what conditions an aggregate credit rule that feeds back only on actual GDP can stabilize consumer prices. The model features heterogeneous households, production and consumption financing, two-sector supply, and bank profit reflux; net credit is linked to the gross financed purchase flow through within-period principal repayment reflux. Two independent disturbances are examined: a shift in the allocation of production financing and a shift in consumption-goods supply. We define the matching gap as the difference between the effective expenditure of displaced consumption financing and the consumption expenditure refluxed from production financing through wages, dividends, and investment output. The structural compatibility theorem states that the same aggregate feedback eliminates the first-order consumer price effects of both disturbances if and only if this gap is zero and the feedback slope satisfies the price-neutrality condition. When the gap is nonzero, consumer prices vary with financing allocation even holding aggregate credit and actual GDP fixed. This yields two price-neutral feedback thresholds and the spacing between them, together with an ordering restriction on the price-output responses of the two disturbances. The gap decomposes into five components: income distribution, investment purchase, physical investment response, repayment reflux, and direct wage financing. We derive primitive conditions under which the gap is strictly positive and a feasible region with positive margin. A full account construction shows that, under the strict K-rule, credit and real output grow together and wage-induced consumption rises, while consumer prices may still decline; reversed configurations indicate the conditions under which the conclusion changes. These results show that an aggregate rule provides only a nominal constraint: consumer price stability additionally requires compatibility among credit use, income reflux, and supply response. The conclusions are local first-order conditions within the stated closure and do not address financial stability or welfare evaluation.

detail.abstract: The Federal Reserve System, created by the Federal Reserve Act of December 1913, has evolved from a modest institution designed to make the supply of currency and credit more elastic into the most influential central bank in the world. This paper examines the role of the Federal Reserve (“the Fed”) along four dimensions: its institutional design and independence, its conduct of monetary policy, its function as lender of last resort and financial stabiliser, and its international position as issuer of the dominant global reserve currency. Throughout, the Fed is compared with three other major central banks: the European Central Bank (ECB), the Bank of England (BoE) and the Bank of Japan (BoJ). The argument proceeds historically and analytically. Drawing on the historiography of Friedman and Schwartz (1963), Meltzer (2003, 2009) and Hetzel (2008), together with the modern theoretical literature on rules and discretion (Kydland and Prescott, 1977; Barro and Gordon, 1983; Taylor, 1993), the paper shows that each of the Fed’s major institutional turning points was a response to a failure: the banking panics of 1930–33, the wartime subordination of monetary policy to Treasury financing, the Great Inflation of the 1970s, the global financial crisis of 2007–09 and the pandemic of 2020. Using official statistics from the Board of Governors, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Bureau of Economic Analysis and the statistical offices and central banks of the euro area, the United Kingdom and Japan, the paper documents how inflation, unemployment, policy rates and central bank balance sheets behaved across these episodes. The comparative analysis suggests three conclusions. First, the Fed’s dual mandate and its unusually decentralised governance make it more flexible than the ECB and the BoE in its response to real-economy shocks, but also more exposed to political contestation. Second, the Fed’s role as a global lender of last resort, exercised through dollar swap lines, gives it a responsibility that its domestic mandate does not recognise. Third, the credibility accumulated since the Volcker disinflation is a stock that can be depleted: it depends on institutional independence that is protected by convention and statute rather than by constitutional entrenchment. The paper closes with policy implications for the framework, the balance sheet, communication and accountability.

detail.abstract: In many stock markets, a handful of firms account for much of market value. We provide the first evidence that such markets have more informative prices and explain why. In 43 economies over 2001-2022, prices in more concentrated stock markets forecast future fundamentals more strongly, including when concentration is instrumented with the largest firms’ relative R&D intensity. For the largest fifth of firms, a ten percentage point higher share of the ten largest firms raises the three-year forecasting slope by a third of its average. The gain comes from how investors’ information choices respond. In our model, investors with market power trade and acquire information. The growth of dominant assets adds supply noise that would make their prices less informative if information choices were fixed. Instead, learning moves toward them, and the largest attract additional informed investors, who lower each other’s price impact and trade more aggressively, so average price informativeness rises. As the model predicts, the gains in the data are larger for larger firms and for firms held more by active investors. The smallest firms’ prices become less informative when the largest firms gain market weight. Concentration among investors has the opposite effect, and market power lets one framework deliver both signs.

detail.abstract:
Rebalancing a portfolio back to fixed weights earns, in the accounting of stochastic portfolio theory, an excess-growth term γ*: one half of the gap between the weighted average variance of the constituents and the variance of the portfolio, also called the diversification return. We ask whether that term can be collected as a trading profit, net of costs, against a benchmark an investor could hold. Eight pre-registered studies, each with its universe, parameter grid, promotion thresholds (the conditions a result must meet before its strategy can be proposed for capital) and controls fixed before scoring, cover crypto majors, a 122-name US large-cap universe (2007-2026, 19.45 years) and an 8-ETF cross-asset basket. As a measurement, γ* is confirmed. In equity the harvest term (the accumulated excess growth, scored net of cost) is +83.9 basis points per year (bps/yr) at a Newey-West t-statistic of +7.32, with a deflated Sharpe ratio of ≈1.000. It is positive in all 20 sample years and stable when the universe is cut to the 30 largest names (+82.3 bps/yr, t = +7.89). On the same arithmetic the theoretical fixed-weight diversification term is +314 bps/yr in equity and +138 bps/yr cross-asset. As a trade, the term fails in every tested form. Against buy-and-hold of identical starting weights the realized rebalancing premium is -68.5 bps/yr in equity (Newey-West t -0.61), -34.9 bps/yr under a size-factor-neutral overlay (0.0th percentile of a random-direction hedge control), and +11.6 bps/yr cross-asset (Newey-West t +0.19, below threshold, and negative in the four-asset robustness cut). It stays below threshold under each of the four conditioning gates tested, where a gate is a rule that switches rebalancing on or off with a market state: a 12-1 momentum gate, a Lo-MacKinlay variance-ratio gate, a gate on the serial correlation of cross-sectional dispersion, and a crypto gate on rising concentration of market weights, which we call dominance momentum. Two of those gates show timing skill against a size-matched random-timing control, which ranks the gate among 2000 random gates that act equally often (99.6th and 98.9th percentiles), and neither produces a tradeable premium. Fixed-weight rebalancing is short a straddle on relative performance (Rattray, Granger, Harvey and Van Hemert 2020): mean-reversion years pay (+1035 bps in 2009, +1247 bps in 2022), trend and concentration years lose (-896 bps in 2023, -1045 bps in 2024), and the annual premiums show 2007-2026 as net trend.
Each headline result is a null or a measurement, so the eight studies yield no tradeable signal; no study authorized capital, and no construction described here has a live track record. What the program hands forward is a candidate turnover governor, by which we mean a rule that tells a portfolio which scheduled rebalances it can skip. Gates with demonstrated timing skill would, if that skill transfers, reduce the cost of rebalancing a book that must rebalance for other reasons. That application was not tested in the eight studies and requires its own forward registration before use.

detail.abstract: The fundamental law of active management (Grinold, 1989) states that the information ratio (IR, active return per unit of active risk) of an optimally combined signal set is IR = IC·√breadth, where IC is the information coefficient of one bet, the correlation of its forecast with the realised return, and breadth counts independent bets. With per-signal information coefficients largely fixed by the anomaly literature, breadth is the binding constraint, yet few treatments make it precise. For the cross-sectional return model r = S a + ε, ε ~ N(0,Σ), with K signals stacked columnwise in S: (i) the signal overlap matrix M = SᵀΣ⁻¹S is the Fisher information matrix of the loading estimate; (ii) the maximum attainable squared information ratio is the Cramér–Rao quadratic form IR(max)² = icᵀM⁻¹ic, where ic is the vector of per-signal information coefficients, and Grinold's law is its orthonormal special case; (iii) effective breadth is the participation ratio of ρ = M(c)/tr(M(c)), with M(c) the correlation form of M (unit diagonal), the reciprocal of the sum of its squared eigenvalues, and the exponential of its von Neumann entropy, the Shannon entropy of those eigenvalues; and (iv) each signal's marginal contribution to the ceiling is a Schur complement, and when signals are added one at a time their contributions telescope exactly to the ceiling. These identities, verified numerically, make the density-matrix description of an ensemble allocator's overlap matrix, absent a regime adjustment, a relabelling of Fisher information (though not of the allocator's weights) and yield a Cramér–Rao-grounded signal-admission criterion, under which a signal is admitted only if its Schur complement exceeds a fixed fraction of the squared ceiling. For a seven-signal library spanning price-, options- and earnings-derived signals on a 66-name market-neutral book, an equicorrelated summary of the library (a common information coefficient of 0.04 from the literature and a pairwise correlation of 0.24 to 0.31 fitted to its two breadth measures) puts the ceiling at 0.063 to 0.068 per rebalance, gross of costs and not computed from the book's own measured coefficients. Three signals put through the admission criterion were marginal, and on that basis we judge those domains built out: a further signal from them would not raise the ceiling materially. The measurements made on the 66-name book are nulls, as is a test of the same geometry as a risk budget. Run on its three price signals alone, the book returned a gross alpha of +0.041% per year (Newey–West t = +0.013). A composite of accounting-fundamentals signals landed at the 5.5th percentile of a null distribution formed by permuting its scores across stocks within each day, against a permutation threshold of the 95th percentile. A risk budget set by the same geometry lost to equal-risk contribution, which gives each stream the same share of portfolio risk, in a pre-registered out-of-sample test over 119 months (2016–2026) on three near-orthogonal return streams (K = 3), with a Sharpe ratio of 1.25 against 1.51.

detail.abstract: Gulen and Woeppel (2026) show that stocks with convex recent price paths earn lower subsequent returns in the US. detail.abstract: A companion paper documents a time-series-momentum sleeve on large liquid crypto assets (the majors): a portion of a portfolio that holds each asset while its trailing return over a fixed lookback (L = 30 days) is positive and holds cash otherwise. That paper's headline result is drawdown control, and we attribute the reduction to the sleeve's trend exit, its sizing construction and a crash-state overlay. Per-asset trend exits brought the invested fraction of the sleeve below 50% within 3–15 days of every market peak that preceded a decline of 30% or more. The sleeve was at most half-invested at the start of 88–90% of the periods in buy-and-hold's lowest tenth by return. Equal weights held only while an asset trends up keep part of the sleeve in cash when trends disagree. The drawdowns of two published variants (−30.2% vs −56.8%) suggest that this explains part of their gap but do not isolate how much, because those figures come from different frames and no same-window test was run. The overlay, which cuts exposure when the aggregate market is deep in drawdown, leaves the Calmar ratio (annual growth over maximum drawdown) roughly unchanged. Protection costs −30.6% per year in calm periods (the sleeve's log return relative to holding) and, larger still, the gains given back when the sleeve re-enters late, as in a 429-day lag after the December 2018 trough. In the two most recent drawdown spells, 39–44% of losses came from re-entry chop, small losses taken on re-entries that fail, well ahead of losses taken while invested in falling markets. An asymmetric lookback that enters faster than it exits, the obvious remedy, was tested in six preregistered variants (arms) and every arm lost. Faster entry did shorten time out of the market, yet the chop share rose monotonically (0.363 → 0.444) because faster re-entry catches more failed upturns than sharp recoveries. Four earlier preregistered attempts (a lookback ensemble, a whipsaw filter, intraday re-entry and learned bet sizing) also returned nulls, so the sleeve's residual drawdown is a cost of the construction that no tested variant removes. The attribution is descriptive and preregistered, and its code reproduced the published full-history figures to the decimal. All results are backtests on a universe tilted toward survivors, and none of the six arms differs from baseline by |t| of 2 or more in sample. Full-sample performance is concentrated before December 2021: in the learned-bet-sizing study's walk-forward evaluation window (December 2021 onward) the sleeve's Sharpe ratio at full size was 0.335, against 1.52 over that study's full sample. No forward validation exists: the model portfolio (run on live prices with no capital at risk) accumulating the sleeve's out-of-sample record was retired on 2026-08-29 with 124 scored rebalance records against a registered requirement of 533, and no verdict was read.

detail.abstract: Democratic stability depends not just on widespread personal commitment to democratic values, but democratic norms: mutual expectations that others will uphold democracy. Scholars fear that, as these norms erode, citizens become more willing to engage in anti-democratic behavior. However, most existing studies measure personal support for democracy, which may only serve as a lagging indicator of norm erosion. And, since erosion happens over time, it cannot be measured in a single cross-sectional survey. To address these challenges, we use an incentivized coordination game to directly measure democratic norms in a panel survey, showing that over the first 100 days of Trump’s second term, Republicans came to expect their co-partisans to express less opposition to undemocratic practices and Democrats came to expect their co-partisans to express less opposition to incivility. Despite this norm erosion, however, neither group showed evidence of changes in their own personal commitment to democracy or civility. We then tested the behavioral implications of this norm erosion using a real monetary donation task. When partisans were presented with evidence of democratic norm erosion in an experiment, Republicans allocated significantly more money to an undemocratic organization. Our findings demonstrate that democratic norms can erode quickly, and this erosion can increase anti-democratic behavior.

detail.abstract:
Experimental evaluation of digital image-processing algorithms poses a fundamental methodological challenge: obtaining input signals whose radiometric, colorimetric, and spatial information is precisely known while allowing them to be processed through the same procedures used by commercial RAW-development systems.

Conventional evaluation methods rely on photographic captures of standardized targets or on synthetic images processed in controlled computational environments. Physical captures, however, incorporate optical and electronic perturbations that are difficult to separate, whereas conventional simulation procedures do not necessarily reproduce the processing conditions associated with camera manufacturers' proprietary RAW formats.

This work presents nefinject, a computational methodology for synthesizing and introducing arbitrary image signals into Nikon Electronic Format (NEF) files while preserving container structure and compatibility with RAW-decoding procedures.

The method integrates an inverse colorimetric model based on dual-illuminant DNG profiles, a Bayer colour-filter-array sampling procedure, optical and optoelectronic perturbation simulators, and a 14-bit Nikon lossless-compression encoder.

The implementation was developed and characterized using files from a Nikon D610 camera, with arrays of $6080\times4028$ samples. The integrity of injected information is verified by numerical comparison between the synthesized mosaic and that recovered by the decoder, with a maximum reconstruction error of zero digital numbers as the acceptance criterion.

In addition, the library enables the construction of reproducible test stimuli, including a synthetic 24-patch ColorChecker Classic and a Siemens star, for characterizing colour reproduction, detail, and spatial artifacts. An evaluation based on CIEDE2000 and resolution measurements is proposed, together with an experimental design that separates the contributions of the optics, sensor, and processing algorithms.

Finally, the implications of this technological capability for digital forensics are examined. The possibility of introducing arbitrary visual content into a structurally valid RAW container calls into question the use of this format as sufficient evidence of photographic authenticity, regardless of whether the content was created by photography, computer graphics, or generative models.

detail.abstract: This article develops a deductive, normative-monist theory of justice grounded in explicit micro-axioms of human nature. Equal human rights-the standing of persons as ends rather than mere means-serves as the singular meta-principle governing legitimate coercion. We establish two foundational analytical dichotomies: first, distinguishing normative justice (the meta-principle of equal rights as benchmark) from real/available justice (the emergent game-theoretic equilibrium under given institutional constraints, where not perfect but "optimal" justice exists); and second, separating moral character (internal self-discipline, or self-binding) from operational justice (discretion-free third-party enforcement, or institutional Tit-for-Tat other-binding). Neutrality is not a fruit of private virtue, but an engineering output forced under detached conditions (𝑎 → 0) and systematically shielded from secular interference. By formalizing institutional regimes through binary justice supply equations-contrasting Rule of Power (J =-1 + 𝑎M) with Rule of Justice (J = 1-𝑎M)-we demonstrate how institutional architecture shifts social payoffs from a Fear of Power to a Fear of Justice, transforming repeated Prisoner's Dilemma interactions from mutually destructive to mutually beneficial equilibria. Optimal justice is scarce because unjust regimes institutionalize reverse rewards and penalties (institutional adverse selection) while demand remains probabilistic and heavily time discounted. Seeking virtuous rulers optimizes the wrong objective function; qualified justice products can be manufactured under strict constraints without saintly natures or eschatological judgment.

detail.abstract: Index realized volatility measures rough on free daily data, and that roughness does not forecast. Absolute-moment scaling of un-smoothed per-bar Rogers–Satchell volatility yields a median Hurst exponent H ≈ 0.061 with scaling-law fits of r² ≈ 0.98–0.998, which is the Gatheral–Jaisson–Rosenbaum rough regime. We take that median across SPY, the S&P 500 cash index, QQQ and IWM (n = 5,416 observations per index, 2005–2026), with per-index exponents from 0.048 to 0.079. Smoothing the proxy inflates the estimate: a five-day rolling mean of the same per-bar variance raises the SPY exponent by +0.19 (0.071 to 0.259; January 1993 to July 2026, 8,423 bars), and the five-day rolling Yang–Zhang proxy of the original pipeline, a different estimator as well as a smoothed one, read +0.345 higher at the four-index median over 2005–2026, enough to fail a roughness test outright. This hazard adds to the Cont–Das "fact or artefact" debate, in the direction opposite to theirs. Our measurement has limits: we ran no placebo of Brownian volatility seen through the same range proxy, and a later note found that daily absolute returns, also un-smoothed, do not recover the exponent (SPY H = 0.016, r² = 0.80, n = 2,901). detail.abstract: We develop an integrated framework to quantify the short-run impacts of carbon pricing on climate and air pollution externalities in the electricity sector. Combining machine learning and chemical transport modeling, we track policy impacts all the way from electricity dispatch and emissions of CO2 and air pollutants at the generating unit to formation of secondary PM2.5, population exposure and associated premature deaths. The abatement channel is coal-togas substitution which occurs within and between interconnected electricity markets. Carbon pricing reduces PM 2.5-related mortality due to co-emissions by 8.9%. Monetized health co-benefits exceed the incremental generation costs by more than €5 billion, implying a net welfare increase in Europe on top of global climate benefits. Counterfactual analyses reveal that net co-benefits per tonne amount to 60% of what is feasible with socially optimal pollution taxes, and that marginal co-benefits are weakly decreasing in the permit price. Overall, our results reinforce the role of cap-and-trade as an efficient policy instrument to internalize both carbon and air pollution externalities of power generation.

detail.abstract: Translation of the bioeconomy vision for Europe into actions relies on how multi-actor partnerships reconcile spatial fragmentation with latent relational capacity. The study explores these challenges through consortium-based analysis of 474 actors in 24 European countries participating in a European partnership, representing among the first attempts to develop a harmonised, multi-country stakeholder mapping framework within a European bioeconomy research and innovation partnership. Through the combination of techniques ranging from mapping to structural reach-engagement positioning, affiliation-based network analysis, and engagement potential, the study reveals a territorial paradox wherein stakeholders' concentration within the consortium-generated register is skewed towards Southern and Central Europe but latent engagement potential is stronger in Northern and Baltic regions. In terms of structural reach-engagement diagnoses, there are discrepancies between the actors' capacity and their willingness to engage in bioeconomy endeavors. Bio-based upstream industries find themselves in an influential though relationally inactive space, whereas primary production and civil society actors express willingness but suffer from low influence. From a network perspective, transactions between actors remain short-lived project-based relationships and collaboration across the value chain remains impossible due to lack of coherence in the value-chain positions and short-term funding structures. It becomes evident that standard engagement procedures are not sufficient to support bioeconomy aspirations of the European Union. The need for transitioning from listing of stakeholders to the ecosystem orchestration strategy becomes evident. Implementing such architectures will strengthen policy legitimacy, accelerate innovation diffusion, and establish resilient governance structures capable of sustaining long-term bioeconomy transitions across diverse European territories.

detail.abstract: We document that CEOs reduce investment, increase net leverage, and expand net share repurchases over their tenure. To explain these patterns, we develop a dynamic model of a firm run by a sequence of CEOs. Each CEO has a finite tenure and chooses investment, financing, and payout to maximize her utility over wealth under a contract that combines a base salary with equity-based pay. The model identifies a new mechanism, the CEO overhang effect, which arises because the CEO's horizon is truncated and future CEOs are also granted equity. As a result, over her tenure a growing share of the returns to the firm's capital and of its costs of debt shifts from current shareholders, including the CEO, to future CEOs. The incumbent CEO therefore underinvests and levers up. She also increasingly repurchases shares, because a larger stake becomes more valuable to her as turnover approaches. Calibrating the model, we infer that the resulting agency cost amounts to 6% of shareholder value.

detail.abstract: We study mechanism design environments in which the designer does not know the distribution of agents' private information and draws inferences from the behavior induced by the mechanism itself. A mechanism is stable if it is optimal under some belief consistent with the information it generates, and robustly stable if this property survives small informational perturbations. We establish a fictitious revelation principle: any incentive-compatible mechanism admits a representation as a direct mechanism paired with an information filter, preserving both outcomes and informational content. Applying the framework to the classic monopoly problem, we show that, under regularity of the true type distribution, robustly stable mechanisms coincide with optimal mechanisms under that distribution, as if it were known to the designer. In general, however, posted-price mechanisms can remain robustly stable at local revenue maxima, so globally suboptimal prices can persist.

detail.abstract: The Federal Reserve is reviewing how far its balance sheet can shrink. This paper argues that the binding constraint is reserve demand, not the absence of a standing lending facility. Using daily money-market data from July 2021 to November 2026, I show that the Standing Repo Facility (SRF) did not cap repo rates on stress dates and did not speed their return to normal, whereas the level of reserves governs stress-date pressure. Since runoff ended, the spread between SOFR and the interest rate on reserve balances turns positive at reserves of about $3.09 trillion, close to the current level of $2.96 trillion, and the recalibrated enhanced supplementary leverage ratio is associated with a fall in reserve demand of about $0.38 trillion. Regular use of the SRF since mid-2025 has coincided with repo rates about 5.5 basis points higher relative to the facility rate, consistent with reliance on it. A path that first lowers reserve demand, through regulation and the management of Treasury cash, could reduce total assets from about $6.7 trillion to about $5.0 trillion (range $4.3-5.7 trillion) without routine central bank lending, with the SRF kept dormant as insurance; the elastic reserves system proposed at Brookings would instead require stress-date lending of about $1.6 to 1.8 trillion. The paper also relates balance-sheet reduction to the policy rate, the fiscal backing of US debt and stablecoin run risk under the GENIUS Act, and proposes indicators for monitoring them together.

detail.abstract: Data-driven governance systems are proliferating worldwide, yet how they are assembled, stabilized, and legitimized inside state bureaucracies remains poorly understood. Drawing on 68 interviews and ethnographic observation of two Chinese data-driven surveillance systems, this article introduces political data work to name the sociotechnical labor through which bureaucrats, technicians, and politicians make algorithmic governance possible. We identify three forms: enrolling data work mobilizes political authority and relationships to secure data; productive data work generates, cleans, and substitutes data by hand; and performative data work stages the appearance of technological sophistication regardless of technical completion. These operate not as a static typology but as a circuit, conditioned by a bureaucracy in which authority is fragmented across agencies while accountability runs upward. Far from neutral inputs, data emerge as outcomes of political negotiation—and the systems built to process them invert their own premise, as human labor expands to sustain an automated appearance rather than being absorbed by it. In making these systems work, political data work also reworks the state, redistributing authority among the agencies it enrolls and renegotiating what each system is for. Data-driven governance thus operates less through automated calculation than as an infrastructure of legitimacy and signaling.

detail.abstract: Kentucky's healthcare workforce is disproportionately exposed to workplace violence relative to workers in other industries. When factors associated with workplace violence are examined, Kentucky performs poorly in measures of mental well-being and the prevalence of drug use, ranking in the top fifth for major depressive episodes, methamphetamine use, opioid misuse, and overdose deaths. These risk factors are especially pronounced in the state's Appalachia region, implying that healthcare workplace violence is likely higher there as well. Recent legislative activity has aimed to improve the safety of healthcare workers. One example is increasing legal penalties for assaulting them. A 2026 bill that would allow hospitals to establish their own police departments passed the Kentucky House; however, hospitals would bear the considerable cost. Other bills proposed that mental health wellness examinations be covered without cost sharing, that opioid antagonists be provided on college campuses, and that Medicaid-related entities be prohibited from denying coverage of non-opioid pain treatments in favor of opioids. Given Kentucky's recent legislative considerations and performance in mental health and drug use measures, there appear to be multiple pathways for Kentucky to influence incidents of violence against healthcare workers. However, there is little evidence as to which interventions will be most effective. The overlap between mental health, drug use, and violence provides common ground for advocates of better mental health, reduced drug use, and safer healthcare workplaces.

detail.abstract: A large-scale collection, storage, and processing of students' and teachers' personal data has occurred as a result of the rapid digitalization of education in India. This has occurred through the use of online learning platforms, digital evaluation systems, and educational technology. The use of such digital innovations raises substantial privacy, ethical governance, and accountability issues, despite their improving accessibility, flexibility, and the effectiveness of educational practices. According to the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, educators are envisioned as empowered, ethical leaders and facilitators of holistic education. Nevertheless, the policy provides only limited operational guidance on ethical data governance and educators' responsibilities in increasingly data-driven educational environments. The purpose of this article is to investigate the ethical regulation of educational data in India, with a specific emphasis on empowering teachers and protecting their privacy in accordance with the NEP 2020. Using an approach that is both doctrinal and analytical, the study draws upon constitutional concepts, the National Education Policy 2020, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023, and ethical insights from Indian Knowledge Systems. According to this argument, teachers are increasingly acting as intermediates and ethical data stewards in digital classrooms. As a result, there is a need for increased legal understanding, ethical competence, and institutional assistance. Informed consent, surveillance-oriented education, algorithmic evaluation, and the digital divide are among the significant challenges identified in this research. The study concludes that, to achieve effective teacher empowerment in the digital age, it is necessary to combine information governance with ethical digital literacy. The purpose of this study is to propose policy-oriented and institutional reforms to incorporate ethical data governance into teacher education and professional development. This will align technology innovation with constitutional values, privacy rights, and the holistic educational vision of NEP 2020.

detail.abstract: We study the reliability of inference in staggered difference-indifferences designs in empirical finance. Our census of articles published in the top three finance journals from 2010 to 2025 shows increasing use of heterogeneity-robust estimators in recent years, while the use of finite-sample refinements to inference remains limited. Many articles rely solely on cluster-robust standard errors for inference and provide little information for assessing their reliability. We further show that the reliability of inference in staggered difference-indifferences designs depends on both the characteristics of the sample and researchers' choice of estimators. These features characterize an interval for the effective number of clusters, which helps us assess when conventional clustered inference may be unreliable for a given estimator and when alternative inference methods should be considered. Evidence from simulations and reanalyses of published studies shows that adapting inference according to the effective number of clusters can affect conclusions about treatment effects and lower false rejection rates. The reanalyses also show that a published finding can be sensitive to the choice of inference even when the point estimate remains unchanged.

detail.abstract: I study how forecasters' under- and overreaction to news varies over time with variance misperception. I measure it by comparing objective variance from statistical benchmarks with subjective variance constructed from derivative prices and survey density forecasts. Individual and consensus forecasts shift toward underreaction when subjective variance is low relative to objective variance, and toward overreaction when it is high. This pattern is pervasive across macroeconomic variables, interest rates and corporate earnings. These findings are consistent with a noisy-information model in which forecasters misperceive their prior uncertainty.

detail.abstract: India's Industrial Disputes Act requires manufacturing plants with 100 or more workers to obtain government permission before laying off, retrenching, or closing. Between 2015 and 2017, four states raised the threshold to 300 workers, the level that has applied nationwide since 2025. Using plant-level data from the Annual Survey of Industries and a stacked difference-indifferences design, I find that measured TFP among plants with 100 to 300 workers rises by 7.6 percent relative to plants of the same size in eleven states that kept the threshold at 100. About half of the gain reflects a change in which plants are in this size range. Plants that arrive in the range after the amendments are more productive than arrivals in the comparison states, and the estimated effect is largest at the bottom of the productivity distribution. I find no evidence that the reform reduces the dispersion of marginal revenue products across plants.

detail.abstract: Since 2012, banks and hedge funds have substantially increased their holdings of U.S. Treasury securities, while pension funds and insurance companies continue to hold most of their assets in equities and corporate bonds. Motivated by this pattern, I develop a macroeconomic model with financial institutions in which banks face a liquidity requirement and pension funds and insurers follow an allocation rule. The liquidity requirement trades off a lower frequency of bank runs against the banks' advantage in holding capital. I calibrate the model to the balance sheets of U.S. institutions, quantify the effects of the requirement and of the allocation rule on asset prices and real activity, and find the liquidity requirement that maximises welfare.

detail.abstract: This article examines how Uzbekistan combines industrial policy with tariff reform on its way to membership of the World Trade Organization (WTO). Official statistics on production, enterprises, technological structure, and foreign trade are read together with the customs reforms of 2025-2026 in order to judge how much room for strategic tariffs the country still has. The analysis shows that industry is the second engine of growth after services, that manufacturing is broad but concentrated in low-and medium-low-technology branches, and that the high tariff wall of the period before 2017 has largely been dismantled. Accession commitments will narrow the remaining room further, so the article argues that industrial upgrading has to rely on temporary, conditional, and performance-based support rather than on high duties.

detail.abstract: Background: Clinical prediction systems deployed in intensive care units (ICUs) are routinely evaluated using discrimination (AUROC, AUPRC), calibration, and Brier score, but no common norm-referenced scale exists for comparing forecast quality across hospitals or patient populations. The Horizon Intelligence Quotient (HIQ) framework provides such a scale for general AI forecasting; extending it to clinical ICU data requires handling right censoring, patient-mix heterogeneity, and repeated within-patient predictions-challenges absent in the original formulation. Methods: We develop a censoring-adjusted, population-transported Brier Skill Score (BSS*) estimator and derive its statistical properties. The estimator combines inverse-probability-ofcensoring weighting (IPCW) to handle right-censored outcomes and competing events with density-ratio covariate transport to map each evaluation hospital's patient mix to a declared target population Q. Under five explicit assumptions (A1-A5), we prove the estimator is unbiased and consistent (Theorem 1) and characterise first-order bias from estimated nuisances (Corollary 1). Cluster-robust standard errors that account for both levels of ICU clustering-windows within patient, patients within hospital-are derived via closed-form influence functions (Propositions 1-2) and propagated through the HIQ* transformation. A norm-versioning protocol with a machine-readable version identifier ensures that HIQ* scores from independent studies are comparable. Application: The framework is specified and pre-registered for two ICU disease tasks: (i) sepsis onset within six hours (Sepsis-3 criteria), evaluated on PhysioNet 2019 Sepsis Challenge data with MIMIC-IV and eICU-CRD as replication datasets; and (ii) KDIGO Stage 1+ acute kidney injury (AKI) within 24 hours, evaluated on MIMIC-IV and eICU-CRD. A randomised reader study tests whether adding HIQ* to a standard reporting bundle improves clinicians' and data scientists' interpretation accuracy for comparative forecast performance. Conclusions: This article is submitted as a Registered Report. The six intellectual contributions are: a formal target-population estimand (C1); proofs of unbiasedness, consistency, and first-order bias (C2-C3); closed-form cluster-robust standard errors and HIQ* reliability formula (C4); a norm-versioning protocol for reproducible cross-study comparison (C5); and a pre-registered interpretive utility trial (C6). HIQ* is a fixed affine transformation of BSS* and therefore carries no independent predictive information; its proposed benefit is interpretive. All HIQ claims are explicitly bounded to a communication function; clinical safety or therapeutic benefit are out of scope without prospective evaluation.

detail.abstract: Green bonds are an increasingly important source of sustainable bank funding, yet little is known about how their issuance affects banks' subsequent lending. Using green bond issuance by European banks matched with syndicated loans and borrowers' environmental performance, we trace the pass-through from sustainable funding to corporate lending and borrower emissions. Following green bond issuance, banks become more likely to provide sustainability-related loans to firms that are already relatively green, both within existing relationships and when forming new ones. However, issuing banks take smaller shares in these loans. At the portfolio level, the increase in sustainability-related lending is accompanied by a decline in conventional lending, such that issuing banks do not expand their own overall syndicated lending to greener firms. Environmental improvements are concentrated among greener firms receiving sustainability-related loans from green-bond-issuing banks. Overall, our findings show that green bond issuance changes how issuing banks structure their lending.
